nodes.label: BACKEND_URL scheme drives HTTPS-only behavior, not NODE_ENV
nodes.rationale: NODE_ENV=production is always set in the Docker image (even for local/LAN/Expo Go testing over plain HTTP), so it cannot signal whether the deployment is really behind TLS. isHttpsDeployment instead checks BACKEND_URL's scheme, and drives both useSecureCookies (a Secure cookie over plain HTTP is silently dropped, breaking sign-in) and whether exp:// origins are trusted (only relevant for non-HTTPS/dev testing).
nodes.norm_label: backend_url scheme drives https-only behavior, not node_env

nodes.label: No hand-rolled JWT verification; Better Auth owns session/token validation
nodes.rationale: The old Keycloak backend had incomplete/disabled JWT audience validation (a CRITICAL finding). This template centralizes session and token validation entirely inside the single Better Auth instance via trustedOrigins and server-side session table lookups, avoiding any ad-hoc JWT-checking code path.
nodes.norm_label: no hand-rolled jwt verification; better auth owns session/token validation

nodes.label: Explicit bounded pg Pool instead of an unbounded pool
nodes.rationale: The old Keycloak backend template shipped an unbounded pg pool, a documented weakness that let a burst of concurrent requests exhaust Postgres connections. max/min/idleTimeoutMillis/connectionTimeoutMillis are set explicitly and meant to be tuned per deployment via env vars.
nodes.norm_label: explicit bounded pg pool instead of an unbounded pool

nodes.label: Shared-Postgres audit trail enables transactional audit writes
nodes.rationale: audit_log lives in the same Postgres database as every domain mutation and auth event, so an audit write (e.g. session.create) can share a transaction with the mutation that triggered it -- the old Keycloak backend could not do this because auth events lived in a separate IdP database.
nodes.norm_label: shared-postgres audit trail enables transactional audit writes

nodes.label: Single central AppError-to-HTTP mapping point
nodes.rationale: app.onError is the only place that maps thrown errors to HTTP responses: any AppError is turned into its mapped status/JSON body, and anything else becomes an opaque 500 so internal details never leak to clients.

nodes.label: drizzle-orm migrator used at runtime instead of drizzle-kit CLI
nodes.rationale: docker-entrypoint.sh runs this script before starting the server. It uses drizzle-orm's migrate() function rather than the drizzle-kit CLI so the production image never needs drizzle-kit or any other devDependency installed.
nodes.norm_label: drizzle-orm migrator used at runtime instead of drizzle-kit cli

nodes.label: ADR-006 (Notification Content Models)
nodes.rationale: Two content models share one notification table: 'system' notifications carry translationKey/paramsJson rendered client-side in the viewer's own language; 'admin' notifications are pre-translated into a translations JSONB blob. targetUserId null means broadcast. Lazy per-user state (notification_state) avoids fan-out writes on broadcast: a missing row means unread/not-deleted, so read/delete only ever upsert one row instead of pre-seeding one per recipient.

nodes.label: ADR-009 (Translations JSONB Registry)
nodes.rationale: Replaced fixed titleDe/titleEn/bodyDe/bodyEn columns with a translations JSONB blob (Record<langCode,{title,body}>) keyed by the shared SUPPORTED_LANGUAGES registry, so adding a new language is a registry entry instead of a schema migration. notification_template lets admins override a system notification's built-in translationKey text; the user.create hook bakes an active override into new notifications at creation time, so editing a template only affects future notifications, not already-created rows.
